utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Hannis. Your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Thank you. Our next witness is Andras Riedlmayer. He's an expert witness, Your Honour, who will testify about cultural destruction and damage to sites in Kosovo. His testimony pertains in particular to paragraphs 77(d), as in David, and to particular paragraphs or subparagraphs in paragraph 72. However, paragraph 77(d) names those municipalities that we'll be talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You say paragraph 72 is also engaged, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Paragraph 77(d) makes reference to a number of mosques that were damaged in municipalities, and it then says "as described in paragraph 72." I can tell you we'll be talking about paragraph 72(a), 72(a)(i), (b), (c), (d), (f), (h)(i), (i), (k), and (m).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Noting that this evidence relates to Count 5 caused me to have another look at the phraseology of Count 5, and there is one peculiarity you might wouldn't to give some attention to. Paragraph 76, which is the principal paragraph re-alleging and incorporating earlier paragraphs makes no reference to paragraph 72, oddly. Now, it doesn't matter for this evidence because you specifically refer to paragraph 72 and subparagraph (d), and it doesn't matter for sexual assault either because you refer to it there, but it may have relevance to (a).

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, under the same reasoning as to (b) then, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well (b) is slightly different because paragraph 75 is already incorporated in 76 --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- and it may be that, for the avoidance of doubt, you should be looking at (b) as well to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see your point, Your Honour. I don't have an answer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where it really bites is in relation to forcible transfer and deportation. It may be technical, of course, but you should, at least at some stage - in fact, sooner rather than later - give consideration to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you for bringing that our attention, Your Honour. We will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Riedlmayer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be placed before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Could you state your name for the record and please spell your last name for us.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: My name is Andras Janos Riedlmayer; R-i-e-d-l-m-a-y-e-r.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, I'd like to ask you briefly about your educational background. I understand that you have a bachelor's degree in history from the University of Chicago.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And after that you obtained two master's degrees. Can you tell us what those are in, when you obtained them, and from where.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I have a master's in Near Eastern Studies from Princeton University, which I obtained in 1972, and I have a master's degree in Library and Information Science, obtained from Simmons College, in 1988.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And currently, what is your occupation or position?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: For the -- for the past 21 years, I've directed the Documentation Centre for Islamic Art and Architect of the Aga Khan Program at Harvard University's Fine Arts Library.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I understand from your prior testimony that you also describe yourself as an art documentation specialist.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, your CV - which, Your Honours, is Exhibit P1790 - contains further details about your educational background and your experience related to this area; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would tender his CV at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Riedlmayer, could you repeat the name of the programme at Harvard University Library.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It is called the Aga Khan Program for Islamic Art and Architect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, since the time your CV was written, I understand there is one additional matter that we might want to draw attention to. Your CV noted that you were a member of the board of directors of the Turkish Studies Association. I understand since that time you've been elected an officer in that organisation; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes. Last November I was elected to a term as president of the Turkish Studies Association.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Very briefly, can you tell us a little bit about what that group is and what it does.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: It's the Premier International Scholarly Association in Ottoman and Turkish Studies.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, could you tell the Court, what does an art documentation specialist do?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Our speciality is precisely what it says: Documenting art and architect as an aid to scholarship in the field; assembling written and photographic evidence of architecture its change over time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm reminded that, since we both speak English, I should pause when you finish an answer and you should pause when I finish a question, just so the interpreters can keep up with us.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Before you worked on the Kosovo project that's the subject of your report in this case, had you done any similar kind of work in the past?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I had been studying the Balkans for more than three decades on an academic level, and throughout the 1990s, I had been looking at the destruction of cultural property in the wars in Croatia and Bosnia. I had written about it and had given talks at international conferences and before a US congressional commission on the subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you give us a little more detail about what you did in connection with that and what parts of the Balkans you were engaged in.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Principally Bosnia. I was moved to study the fate of art, architecture, and other cultural heritage in Bosnia by the news of the destruction of the National Library in Sarajevo, the destruction of the Mostar bridge, and other tragedies that affected both people and culture during the Balkan wars. I'm not sure what you would --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's sufficient. Have you previously testified as an expert before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes, I have, three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us which cases those were in?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I testified twice in the case Prosecutor versus Slobodan Milosevic, once about Kosovo and once about Bosnia; and also in the case, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, sir, do you speak and read any languages that were helpful to your work in the Balkans?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes. I can read and, to a certain degree, speak Serbian/Croatian/Bosnian. I can read Albanian with a dictionary. I'm fluent in Turkish. And I know the major western European languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, how was it that you came to be involved in this project that led to your survey regarding Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Due to my work in the 1990s, looking at the fate of cultural property in the Balkans, when the war broke out in Kosovo in 1998/1999, I was paying special attention as to whether there were similar reports of destruction of cultural property. I did see such reports, both in interviews with refugees and in the various allegations made by the Yugoslav government and others concerning destruction of cultural property. When the conflict in Kosovo ended in early June of 1999, I contacted UNESCO, given that the UN was about to take on the administration of Kosovo and I assumed that UNESCO would take on the culture centre, and asked if they had any special plans to survey what the state of cultural heritage was in the aftermath of the war. I was informed by my contact at UNESCO headquarters in Paris that at the time they had no plans to do this; all their efforts would be concentrated on the education sector. At that point, I contacted various colleagues, found an architect colleague whom I had known from previous professional work by the name of Andrew Herscher, and the two of us applied for a grant to do field-work in Kosovo. Do you wish to have more detail than that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you this, and I think you've partly answered already: How did you come to the idea of a cultural heritage project for Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: All right. I felt that in the aftermath of war it was very important to record what had happened to cultural property for a variety of reasons. One would be to establish a base-line and priorities for conservation and reconstruction; one would be to assist the Tribunal, if possible, in case there is evidence to be gathered of war crimes; and one was simply to contribute to the historical record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just one question, Mr. Riedlmayer. By the time we are talking of now, which is late 1999, I think, had you already been working for the Office of the Prosecutor here in relation to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you define for us what you mean by the term "cultural heritage."

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Cultural heritage, in the broadest sense, is the cultural and artistic production of peoples, whether it is the written word, works of art, or the built environment. The cultural link has to do, of course, both with the creativity involved and with a connection with the cultural and spiritual life of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, you mention you had contacted an individual you knew by the name of Andrew Herscher to help you work on this. Who was he, or who is he?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Andrew Herscher, H-e-r-s-c-h-e-r, at the time was a trained architect and was in the last stages of finishing his doctorate at Harvard University in architectural history, theory and criticism. He had been involved in documenting cultural destruction in the Balkans before in Mostar, in Bosnia, after the end of the Bosnian war. He had a reading knowledge of Serbo-Croatian and expressed an interest in the project.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you mentioned earlier that the two of you applied for a grant. I take it you didn't have the means to fund this project on your own.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: We did not. We found a foundation, the Packard Humanities Institute, that was willing to give a subvention to cover the expenses of our field-work, and Harvard University was willing to act as the institutional sponsor. We worked through the Centre for Middle Eastern Studies.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us briefly, what is the Packard Humanities Institute?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: The Packard Humanities Institute is a registered charity in the United States. It is involved in various cultural preservation projects in Europe and elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, at the outset, what were the goals that you and Mr. Herscher had in mind for this project?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Our goals, quite simply, were to go to Kosovo and look at every published and otherwise available allegation concerning attacks on cultural and religious heritage and to document it. It sounds like an ambitious project, but Kosovo, you should keep in mind, is a relatively small and compact territory. In order to do this efficiently, we spent the summer, meaning the three months before we launched our expedition in October of 1999, compiling documentation available on heritage in Kosovo so we would know what we were looking for once we got there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what sources did you go to to gather this documentation?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: In terms of published documentation, we are very fortunate that Harvard University has a very rich library and that Kosovo, being part of the former Yugoslavia, had all the cultural institutions of the federal structure of Yugoslavia. So they had an institute for the protection of monuments, they had a provincial museum, they had various other bodies, all of which issued annuals and other publications, documenting cultural heritage in Kosovo. And Harvard had most of these publications. We systematically compiled all the information available on various sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I see the title of your report or your survey is "The Destruction of Historical Culture in Kosovo 1998/1999." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes, "The Destruction of Cultural Heritage," yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So is "historical culture" interchangeable with the term "cultural heritage"?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I don't think the term "historical" appears in the title.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Would that cultural heritage include both religious and non-religious sites?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you began your project, were you and/or Mr. Herscher aware of the different primary religious groups or communities in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what were those, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: The three major traditional -- religious traditions in Kosovo were Islam, which was the religion of most of the Albanian majority; Roman Catholicism, which was the religion of the minority among the Albanians, as well as some other smaller minorities; and Serbian Orthodoxy, which was the traditional religion of the Serb inhabitants of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting. Before we get into detail on this, I was trying to understand your reference there, Mr. Hannis, to "historical culture". Now, I don't see that in the title of the report, nor in the copyright tag to the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I think that's just an error in my notes. It is -- "Cultural Heritage" is the title in his report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Just in case we go off on a tangent later when we're trying to re-assemble this material. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No. My apologies to the Court and the witness; I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Riedlmayer, you mentioned the three religious communities. Can you tell us with regard to each, what type of religious buildings did you associate with each group?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes. In the case of Islam, the main houses of worships were, of course, mosques. These came in two varieties. One, locally called Xhamija, was the congregational mosque. This is the mosque where Friday prayers are performed once a week. There were also smaller mosques called locally Masjid. These often didn't have a minaret, a minaret being like a steeple where the call to prayer is sounded. And these were used for daily prayers but not usually for Friday prayers. In addition, many Kosovar Muslims also followed the Sufi mystical tradition, and there were Teqe, or Tekija, which were Dervish lodges where the Sufi ceremonies would be performed. In addition, there would be the tombs of venerated religious scholars and other holy men and women, and other subsidiary buildings, such as religious schools for Koran readers, and so forth. Also, all three religions revolve around scripture and its study, so all three religions maintained religious libraries and records/archives. In terms of the Serbian Orthodox church, they had, of course, churches. They also had monasteries. They also had their theological school in Prizren and, of course, the normal panoply of parish records and religious libraries. The Catholic church, which was institutionally the smallest in Kosovo, similarly had churches and convents and religious schools.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, you described earlier, I think, the preliminary work that you and Mr. Herscher did to try and select sites. One approach that you might have taken was to try and investigate every known site from every source in Kosovo. Did you try to do that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: We, of course, tried to compile at the very beginning the maximal list of items that could be investigated and the maximum amount of information just so that we would not encounter surprises; however, our field-work was focused primarily on those sites in which there had been allegations of damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you recall now a rough number of sites about which you had discovered allegations of damage?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you that we visited in person approximately 144 sites in the course of three visits to Kosovo, each lasting about three weeks. In addition, we compiled information from sources we judged to be reliable, mostly in terms of photographic documentation. And we have a database in excess of 500 records, which I believe has been submitted to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. So after you and Herscher had gathered this information, you made your first site visit.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When did that take place?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: We went to Kosovo at the beginning of October of 1999, so that's roughly four months after the end of the conflict, and spent about three weeks there through the end of the month. Subsequently, we went for follow-up visits in October of 2000 and March of 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Before actually arriving in Kosovo that first time in October 1999, did you have any contact with this Tribunal or the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes. When we first contacted the Office of the Prosecutor to ask whether the data we collected would be of any interest to them, they expressed an interest and urged us to stop at The Hague on our way to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you do so?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: We did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you advise them of what you and Mr. Herscher had in mind?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: We did, and in turn they advised us, in general terms, as to what sort of thing would make for useful information for them in terms of how to go about documenting. So, for example, they advised us that it would be useful if we could look out for recent pre-war pictures in order to contrast with any post-war documentation. They advised us to do our best to be neutral and impartial in our observations. They advised us that, while they would happily look at our documentation, we would not be acting as agents of the Tribunal; and that the Tribunal office in Pristina could advise us on security conditions but otherwise could not offer us practical assistance. We did all that, and I believe the documentation we compiled complied with these general guidelines. At no time did they suggest what our conclusions should be or what sites to pick or how to proceed about our documenting in technical terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did they have any input on the final report that you wrote?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: They did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, you've told us how you started your work by compiling the list of sites based on published literature or on cultural heritage in Kosovo and a list of those about which there were reports or allegations of damage. With that information in hand, how did you and Herscher go about doing things? What was your methodology when you arrived in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I can give you a brief outline of how we would go about documenting a site. Each day we would draw up a list of sites that we could visit based largely on simple geography, obviously. Communications in the aftermath of war were very difficult. The roads were in a terrible state. There were people still coming back, refugees clogging the roads, so getting about was a real problem. When we got to a site, the first thing we would try to do is identify the site. We would not rely on just passers-by, but we would, first of all, compare the site to whatever pre-war documentation we had. In the case of a building that was completely torn down, the foundations would often still be visible and we would very often have some kind of a ground plan that would be helpful. If there were pre-war photographs, you could often see other buildings and structures in the background with which to compare it. We had spent the three months before the war not only compiling documentation but also trying to establish contacts within Kosovo, to get in touch with heritage professionals there who could provide us with guidance as to where these sites were. On a number of occasions, we managed to get people to accompany us to the sites which saved us considerable time. Once we identified a site, we would then take photographs from various angles, and then Mr. Herscher and I would try to agree on a qualification and description of the damage. And then we would move on to the next site. If, in the process of documenting, we encountered people who claimed to have seen what happened, our instructions from the Office of the Prosecutor were that we were not authorised to depose people; we're not lawyers. But we were to collect basic information, what sort of thing they claim to have known, particularly the time, if they knew it, of when the destruction occurred; and not specifically what person did it but, you know, if they could remember what uniform people might have been wearing. And then we would take their contact information, which we included in our report, and it was up to the Tribunal to contact them. Then we would move on to the next site. We generally were out from before 6.00 in the morning often until late at night, and then once back in Pristina, we would compile the day's documentation and try to organise it. And once we got back to Cambridge, then we started putting it, together with our photographs, into a database.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just one --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- again, it's a minor matter, but you started that by telling us you spent three months, you said, "before the war not only compiling documentation but also trying to establish contacts within Kosovo, to get in touch with heritage professionals." Do you mean three months after the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Three months after the war. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I have just a little query. Did you meet any of the Sufis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, certainly. Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: And were they available?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some were, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: And did they follow the Turkish Rumi?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. There are a variety of mystical orders active in Kosovo. The followers of Rumi, the Bektashi, are not among them. There are orders, such as the Rufai, the Sa'adi, and others. In Western Kosovo, there is also the Bektashi tradition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: No Christian Sufi?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Christian religious orders are associated with the Orthodox and Catholic church respectively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Riedlmayer, as part of your project, when you discovered what appeared to be damage or destruction, I understand that you and Herscher came up with a system to rate it or assess that damage. How did you decide on what standard you were going to use?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: We had a scale of destruction which we initially tried to model on the scale used by the UNHCR, the United Nations Office of the High Commissioner for Refugees. The problem with that was the UNHCR scale was very specifically oriented towards emergency reconstruction of shelter and so the categories tended to be based on criteria, such as the state of the infrastructure, plumbing, electricity, the number of bedrooms; in other words, criteria that were not easily applicable to historical buildings or houses of worship. Then we looked at other criteria that were used, for example, in the assessment of buildings in Dubrovnik and Dalmatia following an earthquake back in the 1960s and 1970s, and we came up with a list of criteria that pretty much matched the UNHCR scale but was reduced to criteria that could be established through strict visual observation without resorting to technical tests. I can go through the criteria, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will. Let me ask you a couple of questions first. So I take it there was not an existing standard for assessing damage to cultural, historical buildings?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes. There were multiple scales in use, none of them particularly applicable to this post-war situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So can you explain to the Court what standards you and Herscher came up with, and how you distinguished one from another.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes. Our scale began with, of course, "undamaged," which is self-explanatory, a building that either shows no signs of damage and also shows no signs of recent reconstruction. Then, the first damage category was "lightly damaged," and we were very conservative in its application. In other words, this could be any building that had not sustained damage that seriously structurally compromised it. This could be anything as light as vandalism and small fire set inside, you know, holes in the wall from projectile impacts, to even the demolition of a church steeple or a mosque minaret, as long as it did not completely collapse the roof or cause a structural element to fail. The second category in the damage category is "heavily damaged." Heavily damaged would be one or more principal elements of the building had been impaired. So, for example, one of the perimeter walls had collapsed, or typically a building would be burned out or the roof collapsed. And very often there would be a combination of damage to various parts of the building. The third category would be "almost destroyed." Almost destroyed means the building was essentially a total loss, but there were still some identifiable parts of the structure standing above ground. And "completely destroyed" would be a building of which no identifiable parts were left standing, a pile of rubble or sometimes a completely cleared site.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In those cases of a completely cleared site, how were you able to determine that there had been some building there before?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Well, one way to do it is, seeing as this was only four months after the war, there hadn't been time for extensive growth of vegetation or weathering, and so you could very often still trace foundations. The other way to do it is to take a very careful look at before-photographs and try to match up buildings in the background.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, I think you told us before that you made three trips in all to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How long did it take you and Herscher to complete this survey?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: We took approximately two years to finish the survey, or three trips. As I mentioned before, they took approximately three weeks each.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you, I think, told us earlier that you and Herscher personally visited 144 sites.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How many of those did you see jointly?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Almost all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how did you go about making the assessment? If there were just two of you working together, did you have to agree before you would assign a value?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you have any examples where you and he disagreed?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us about one and how you resolved it.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Certainly. On our first site visits in the town of Vucitrn, north of Pristina, we saw a series of mosques whose minarets had been shot off. They had been severed near the bottom and had collapsed onto the roof of the adjacent mosque. And the falling masonry had crashed through the roof and made a big hole in the roof and obviously caused damage to the roof and the interior. And I had been inclined to say that this constituted "heavily damaged" and Mr. Herscher, who was intent on keeping the categories very conservative, pointed out that, even though the minaret was gone and the roof was partially smashed in, the mosque was still essentially structural intact. The perimeter walls were standing and two-thirds of the roof was still okay. And so we discussed it and he prevailed and we called those "lightly damaged."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And of the two of you, he's the architect.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: So I deferred.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, I think you told us before you started you had a list of over 500 sites.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we subtract 144 from 500-and-some, there is more than 350 that you and Herscher were not able to visit personally.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What about those sites that are in the survey? What were your sources for information about them?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: We were very fortunate that we were able to obtain a lot of photographic documentation from several sources that we judged to be reliable. The largest number of photos and other information that we got came from the International Management Group. This is an inter-governmental agency, that on a contract from the Council of Europe, was doing a municipality-by-municipality survey of infrastructure in Kosovo. The main goals of the survey were to assess the state of public facilities, such as clinics and schools and other public facilities; but, to our relief, they also included a category of religious and heritage sites. They compiled a database, which I submitted along with our report, which contained a great deal of photographic and other information on these sites. The assessments they made were not always consistent or reliable, from our standpoint, given that their different teams in different municipalities didn't seem to have consistent standards as to what they would call, say, 20 per cent damaged. In some cases, that would mean a building that had had its windows smashed in; in other places, it would have been a building that would have been completely burned out. So what we relied on primarily was their photographs, to which we applied our own criteria. The second largest group of photographs we obtained came from the three religious communities. The Islamic community of Kosovo, which is the coordinating body for the Muslim congregations within the province, had compiled in the immediate aftermath of the war a very large archive of several hundred photographs, showing mosques that had been damaged in the war. Also, from them, we acquired a set of a journal they had published in the 1990s called Dituria Islame, which had many pre-destruction photos of mosques published, and since they were published, they were easily dateable.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you spell the name of that publication.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. That's D-i-t-u-r-i-a, new word, I-s-l-a-m-e, something like "Islamic Knowledge."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: It's a religious monthly. The Serbian Orthodox church was also very active immediately after the war documenting the fate of its religious structures, many of which were damaged particularly in the summer after the war. And they published a work called "Crucified Kosovo" and also maintained a number of web sites. We were also in contact -- direct contact with clergymen from the Serbian Orthodox church, such as Father Savo Janjic, who was known as the cyber monk because he -- at a time when you couldn't call Kosovo by telephone, you could e-mail him. So we exchanged photographs by e-mail. The Roman Catholic church, which was the smallest of Kosovo's three religious communities and whose buildings had suffered the least damage, did not have any publications, but we were able to interview several parish priests who informed us about the state of religious monuments in their particular corners of Kosovo. The Catholic church also had a number of publications from before the war which provided pre-war photos of these surges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, the IMG that you referred to, International Management Group, were they active only after the war or were they already active in the area before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were only active after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Before I move on from the religious communities, did you have a liaison with a particular individual or a particular office for each of those communities, or did you just randomly contact individuals?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Well, we were very fortunate because, seeing as we were in Kosovo in the immediate aftermath of the war, Kosovo being a very small and geographically compact place, you couldn't help but bump into the people who were involved in various kinds of reconstruction-oriented work. And while in Pristina we attended the weekly conferences held by UNHCR, to which all these agencies were involved. So that's how we got in touch with International Management Group. The clergymen we sought out on our own, and I was about to get to the non-religious organisations -- would you like me to continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: There is, as I mentioned, an Institute for the Protection of Monuments of Kosovo. It's a central body based in Pristina. Their archives were evacuated to Serbia after the war, so they didn't have a great deal of documentation, but some members of the institute had gone out and done some documentation on their own and they shared their photographs with us. In addition, we were able to obtain other photographs from local agencies. There was an Institute for the Protection of Monuments in Djakovica, or Gjakova, in Western Kosovo, and they had documentation. The United Nations Administration in Kosovo had a regional office in Pec, or Peje, in north-western Kosovo, which had also undertaken a project in the year after the war to document what happened to historic civil architecture in that region and we collected that material. So we collected information from a variety of sources, which are listed in an appendix to our report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I believe those are contained in appendix 2.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The Institute for Protection of Monuments of Kosovo, what kind of agency was that? Was that a private or a governmental institution; do you know?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: It was a governmental institution at the provincial level, at the level of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Pre-existing before the war?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The local institute in Djakovica, what about that? Is that private, governmental?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: It was municipal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And pre-existing before the war?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In addition to those, you had some information from private sources, private individuals.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What about the media as a source?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: At no time did we include a site or document a site based exclusively on media sources; however, we did comb all the media reports for first-hand reports of damage. This, we thought, was important, largely in pinning down the time of damage. If a reporter had passed by a site at a particular date and noted that the roof was missing or the minaret was toppled or the church was collapsed, then we knew that it was at least damaged as of that date. Similarly, if the report says it was intact, we noted that. So in -- it was helpful in corroborating other kinds of evidence that we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I think I read that part of your requirement for making an assessment regarding damage required a photo.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is that just one photo of the damage or a photo of the pre-existing condition or both?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Well, preferably both, but failing a pre-war photo, at least a photo of the damaged building. You know, there is a lot you can tell from a damaged building from a photograph, so you don't always need the pre-existing photo. That's the optimal. We also got very fortunate with regard to pre-existing photos because, through our research, we found a gentleman in Prizren named Raif Virmica. His name is mentioned in the report. He was a local journalist who had -- who was a private scholar and had developed an interest in the heritage of Kosovo and had published a number of books on it. And because he had published these books privately, his address was in the back. So on a chance we looked him up and he turned out to have a private archive of hundreds of photographs, many of them taken just a year before the war with a camera with a date stamp. So we were able to use his photos, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you spell his last name for me and the court reporter.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Sure. His first name is R-a-i-f. His last name is V, as in Victor, i-r-m-i-c-a.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I want to ask you about damage to Islamic religious heritage, and you've described some of the buildings that fall into the category of religious buildings. Was there a particular type among those several various kinds that seemed to be most frequently damaged?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Well, the most publicly visible Muslim institution is, of course, the mosque, which generally has a tall minaret. It's slim, steeple-like structure, which both serves a symbolic function pointing to the heavens, testifying to the unitive God, but also a practical function, that's where the call to prayer is issued from. And it's usually at the centre of a given village or neighbourhood. And we had, from that journal I mentioned, a statistic published before the war, in 1993 I believe, that at that point there were 607 mosques in all of Kosovo. Of these, we found documentation or, through our site visit, evidence that at least 225 had been destroyed or damaged during 1998/1999, so over a third of all mosques in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In connection with that, how were you able to determine that the damage to those 225 had occurred during that time-period in 1998/1999? How did you do that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Well, the date of damage, of course, can be determined in various ways. First of all, let me stress, we were there after the war so we are in no sense eye-witnesses to anything but the aftermath. We were not there to watch the destruction. However, first of all, it was relatively easy to tell whether a building had been recently damaged. I mentioned before evidence of weathering and growth of vegetation. If a building had been burned down relatively recently, you could see freshly burned wood, marks of soot that hadn't been washed away by the rain. You know, even the smell was still quite persistent a few months after the war. Obviously, if a building had suffered damage quite visibly from projectiles, you know, huge blast holes in the wall or marks of bullets all over, I think it would have been a fair conclusion that this is not something that happened in peacetime. Through the journalists' reports, through any eye-witnesses who came forward, and, of course, any information we obtained from the affected religious communities, all of that we included in our report and sourced it carefully. And obviously it's up to the Court to determine how reliable these reports are as to date.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In addition to those physical sites you described, when you went out and saw the damage, the one other thing that might assist you in dating that would be the date of the most recent photograph of a site where it was still standing intact?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes, and that's one of the reasons we were very eager to find pre -- recent pre-war photos, if possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In your report you state that much of the damage to these mosques was "clearly the result of attacks directed on the mosque." Can you tell us why you made that conclusion, as opposed to being collateral damage or something else.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: In all of our site reports, we include a category for context, "context" meaning the condition of its closely neighbouring or surrounding buildings. Obviously, in the case of a building that is isolated, standing in the middle of countryside, that is not an issue. But most of these buildings were in fairly densely built-up settlements. And in each case, we noted whether neighbouring buildings showed any damage. We also looked at things like what the nature of the damage was. Obviously, if a building showed lots of impacts of small-arms fire, there's -- it was plausible that it had been caught in the middle of a battle. If the only damage to the building was the minaret having been blown up, and often with signs that it had been blown up with explosives packed inside, the minaret has internal staircase, and when it is blown up in that fashion often the structure often balloons out, flares out. And you can see sometimes the powder marks as the blast expands. That kind of damage is clearly not accidental; it's intentional.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mention, I think, that there were some 607 mosques from 1993. Do you recall how many of those were still active -- in active use in 1999?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I don't have the report in front of me, but as I recall it was 590-odd. So it's almost all of them were still in use.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think your number may indicate 568, does that sound about right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Well, that's plausible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I want to contrast or go to the damage to Roman Catholic religious sites. First of all, in general, can you tell us number-wise, in rough figures, what was -- what were the relative figures in terms of Islamic sites, Roman Catholic, and Serbo-Orthodox. Which was the most numerous?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Well, the numbers reflected the make-up of the population. The great majority of the population in Kosovo was Albanian, and the great majority of the Albanians were traditionally adherents of the Islamic faith. So there were more standing mosques than there were standing churches. The minority among the Albanians that was Catholic was a relatively small minority; it may be 10 per cent or so. And Catholic settlements tended to be grouped in particular areas of Kosovo. So we're talking at a relatively low number. In between the two lies the number of Serbian Orthodox churches. Kosovo is, of course, a historic centre of the Serbian Orthodox church and contains some of the most famous and revered structures of Serbian Orthodox religious architecture. The number of these that is in actual use, or was in actual use before the war, was relatively smaller. And so we're talking about some hundreds of buildings; many of them humble village churches, some of them major works of art.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Before I move on, I wanted to ask you a question about Kosovo Albanian, I guess, I would say civilian architecture. Kullas, k-u-l-l-a-s, can you tell us what those are; describe them for us.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Kulla -- the word kulla actually means tower. And what it is, it is a traditional Albanian dwelling, peculiar, really, to the area of and nearly adjacent territories in Montenegro and Macedonia. These were built mostly in the 18th and 19th century. They're quite splendid stone structures, usually built in groups and villages and housing - excuse me - and often housing multiple generations of a clan or extended family.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We've had some in the testimony, earlier in this case, describing -- describing, I think, what you've just talked about as sort of compounds; it's several buildings joined together and surrounded by walls?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes. They're often in a group. A typical village like that would be Nivokaz, which is N-i-v-o-k-a-z, north of Djakovica, which had maybe 20 or 30 of these in several compounds. Decani is another community that was famous for an old town that was essentially composed entirely of kullas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think perhaps you should spell Nivokaz again for us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yes, N-i-v-o-k-a-z.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In the Milosevic trial, I understand there was some issue about the origin, or the attribution, of these to a particular culture. And there was an issue about whether it pertained to Kosovo Albanians or to some other group. Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes. In cross-examination, Mr. Milosevic kept insisting that these were not really Albanian architecture, that, in fact, there were also Serbian kullas. And, among other things, he cited an article by Mark Krasnici, M-a-r-k, K-r-a-s-n-i-c-i, or the Albanian spelling could be K-r-a-s-n-i-q-i, who, back in 1958, wrote a seminal article about kullas. And at the time I hadn't been familiar with the article, given that it was published so long before the war, but I looked it up since. And it was interesting that, on the very first page of the article, Mr. Krasniqi says that kullas in Kosovo are built, primarily, by Albanians. And, as such they, they are regarded as an ethnic symbol; a fact which has contributed to their popularity and spread in the region. More significantly, perhaps, in 1996, so just three years before the Kosovo war, the Republican Institute for the Protection of Monuments of Serbia in Belgrade published a work on vernacular architecture in Serbia by Jovan Krunic, who is one of the leading scholars in that field in Serbia. And the title of the article on kullas is "Siptarska kulla u Mehotija"; the Albanian "Metohija" being the Serbian name for the western part of Kosovo. So clearly there was a recognition among scholars, both Albanian and Serbian, and by the Institute for the Protection of Monuments of Serbia, that the kulla was an Albanian ethnic symbol.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I wanted to now go to your survey and talk about some particular sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a hard copy of the materials I wanted to show the witness. It may be easier for him to follow along with that because there are a number of pages I will be referring to. If I could hand him that. And then the first e-court item I want to put on the screen will be Exhibit P1799.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, the report that we have, I think, is P1789.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that a version for this case rather than the entire report? Or is that the entire --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's the entire report. You should have received a CD in connection with that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I've received --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you a hard copy of the report, the body of the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is a report which runs to 25 pages and then has attachments relating to particular sites. Is that correct? It's a report running to about 25 pages and then there are a series of attachments relating to particular sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. You'll see in the -- you have a copy of the witness notification?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You'll see that the disk that was provided to the Court contains a series of ERN numbers. The report itself is sort of in the middle of that list of ERNs --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But all of these extracts are in the report with the exception of the very first one, I think, which relates to Orthodox damage. What I'm trying to establish, Mr. Hannis, is whether everything that was done by Mr. Riedlmayer has been presented as part of this package of material, or whether, when it comes to looking at individual buildings, you have been selective and have included only the ones that are relevant to this indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the study contains all of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What I intend to show him are the photographs and the selected pages pertaining to those that are listed in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So if you take P1789, on your summary --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- you've identified the page numbers as well, these ERN numbers --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- for the documents which comprise P1789.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that a selective list from the report that Mr. Riedlmayer presented to the OTP, or is it the entire report?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's the entire report, Your Honour. And you will see, if you compare the numbers, for example, Exhibit P1788, which has the English ERN of K020-9391 to 9393, is listed as one of the ERN ranges under Exhibit P1789.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. I think that applies to virtually all of this other material. And what I've printed off as a result of that doesn't cover anything like the total number of buildings I expected would be in the full report; that's why I asked the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, there is a database that was associated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- with this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that. But what I printed off seems to be a limited selection of sites which apply to the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And may I inquire, did Your Honour print off all of the ERNs under this exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, what's under P1789, because the rest is duplication.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. The difference is, Your Honour, some of the enlarged photographs have a different number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed, and they did not print off, I have to say, but I was able to establish what they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Anyway, please carry on. Perhaps it will become clearer as the questions proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May I -- let me see. If we could have Exhibit P1799 on screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, do you see that photograph on the screen before you?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court what that is.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes, that is the Carsiska Xhamija, the market mosque in the centre of Vucitrn. It's a photograph taken in 1998 just before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: And since I assume you will show for the next picture the picture of the site, please note, Your Honours, to the left of the mosque, in the background, is a tall building with a single window underneath the eaves. You will see it in the next photo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I believe there are three or four more pages with this particular exhibit number. If we could go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Okay. You will see the same building in the background, and in the front you can see the remains of the foundations of the mosque and the steps that used to lead up to the door of the mosque. This is a photo that we took during our first field trip in Kosovo in October of 1999, and the triangular space in the centre of town where the mosque had stood and around the mosque, the traditional Albanian goldsmiths bazaar had been completely burned down. You can see traces of burned structures, and then leveled with a road grader, the remains of which could still be seen off to the side. Surrounding this square on all sides were tall, modern buildings, which showed no sign whatsoever of damage, for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you said the remains of which could be seen off to one side, you're talking about the remains of the building or --

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Of the road grader.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Of the road grader.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Of the remains of the building what you see is what was left, basically some charred beams and some rubble here and there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I moved a little too fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we go back to page 1 of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, I'll ask the usher to assist you and hand you an electronic pen with which you can actually touch the screen and mark on the photograph. Could you mark on this photograph, page 1 of Exhibit 1799, the building that you talked about that appears in the next paragraph.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we take a screen shot of that and give it the next IC number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC87, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now could we go to page 2 of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, likewise, on this photo, could you use the pen again and mark that same building.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can we take a screen shot of that and give it the next IC number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC88, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, any other comment on that photo before we move on to the next one?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we go to page 3 of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what is on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: This is another mosque in Vucitrn, the oldest mosque in town. The mosque itself was built in the 15th century, in the 1400s, and it's a photo taken immediately from the adjacent street. You can see in the foreground the edge of a wall. We're standing in the street looking over into the yard of the mosque. The minaret has been sheered off and has collapsed on the mosque. According to local residents, the mosque was -- the mosque minaret had been shot off by a tank cannon from a tank that was just where this photograph was taken from.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How would you and Mr. Herscher describe the damage pictured here?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: We qualified this as a lightly damaged building.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the previous one we saw, that was a completely damaged example?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Completely destroyed, because there was no visible sign of the building left.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this is.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: This is the Karamanli mosque in Vucitrn, the third of Vucitrn's three mosques. K-r-a-m-a-n -- no, I'm sorry, K-a-r-a-m-a-n-l-i. The Karamanli mosque in Vucitrn. And it has suffered a similar fate. The minaret, you can still see the base of it and you can see the rubble, both on the ground next to the mosque and smashed through the roof.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And this would also be characterised as lightly damaged?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: This is the one that Mr. Herscher and I had the argument about but he won; it's lightly damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I think one more page to this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell what this is.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: This is the interior of the Karamanli mosque with the rubble of the minaret that has fallen through the roof.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall when these photographs were taken in Vucitrn?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: In October of 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, if we could go to Exhibit P1788.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in compiling your report, Mr. Riedlmayer, did you establish a database in which to keep all this information?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when we have this next document on the screen, can you tell us if this is a page from the database?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Explain how you decided what kind of information to put in there and where you obtained the information to input.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first field is --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Ivetic is up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I had some time to locate this one in my set of exhibits. I do have an objection that I will be making with respect to the extracts from the study relating to the various sites. This one, in particular, I had to verify to make sure that this was one of the ones I have an objection to; I do. As to the admission of the document and any testimony relating to what other people or other sources indicated to him insofar as this document, I believe, is objectionable under the same standards that we have applied previously to Under Orders and to the As Seen, As Told books, namely, that they are an attempt by the Prosecution to introduce, pursuant to Rule 92 -- improper use of 92 bis, written statements alleging acts and conduct of individuals that are not under oath, in many cases are not even identified. In this case, we do have the identity of some of the informants who provided the information, but, in any event we have heard testimony here today that the OTP, prior to Mr. Riedlmayer going to the site, instructed him not to depose people, that they would be deposed subsequently. And I presume the logical follow-up to that would be if they had information to provide that was credible, they would be brought here as witnesses. Many, if not all, of the persons named as informants or sources for this information in these written extracts or reports are not, in fact, on the witness list and are not being brought here for the ability for confrontation and cross-examination. And therefore, the written reports, the extracts thereof, suffers from the same defect and flaw as we saw in Under Orders and in As Seen, As Told, namely, that it provides statements of persons that the OTP itself, in its instructions to Mr. Riedlmayer, knew it could not utilise as evidence in trial. And now the same Office of the Prosecutor is presenting this document in written form as its only evidence for how these buildings and objects were damaged and when they were damaged. I believe Mr. Riedlmayer can testify as to what he saw and what the damage was that he saw, but I believe once we start going into the cause of the damage and, in particular, if the cause is said to be intentional, the manner and the perpetrators of said damage, that I believe we are going outside the bounds of any type of expertise or knowledge that he might have and therefore are falling into a trap and into an area that I believe should be inadmissible. I can get up for the -- I have gone through each of the extracts and have marked what I believe to be areas that are objectionable based upon this, and so if Your Honours are, indeed, inclined to rule that way, I could, with the Prosecutor, meet and have these exhibits redacted because I believe, again, that it's a portion of the exhibits that is objectionable and is, in fact, improper evidence to be led in any form. So I just wanted to make Your Honours aware of that and, in particular, with this one, with the Vucitrn, I do have some items in here that are, indeed -- that, indeed, fall into this category of written statements by persons who are available as witnesses but who are not being called as witnesses that do not comport to the requirements of the Rules of this Tribunal for written evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. First of all, hearsay is admissible. I think this report -- these reports can be distinguished from As Seen, As Told in some ways. First of all, the collectors of the information in this case are basically, as I understand it, two individuals - Mr. Riedlmayer and Mr. Herscher - so there's some consistency in their approach. We would urge Your Honours not to accept Mr. Ivetic's motion or objection at this time, but decide at the end of the case, when you've heard all the evidence, about how much weight to give these reports. For example, in this case, the information about how a particular minaret was destroyed is from an individual who says that it was shot by a tank. If the visual information concerning the destruction appears consistent with that, if other evidence shows in the case that on that date or that week in April or May of 1999, a particular VJ military unit was in the area and other evidence shows that the only entities that had access to the tanks at that time were VJ, then you may give more weight to that hearsay information from an informant who said it happened that way. But I think it's premature for the Trial Chamber to throw that out at this point without waiting until you've heard all the other evidence. You're professional Judges and you can decide whether or not that's something you have to erase from your mind later on because there's been no other evidence and you decide to give it no weight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, can you assist me, just to be clear, of the exact status of what we're looking at. We have this report which, as I say, has a narrative content of about 25 pages. There is then a database related to it. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, and we intended for Your Honours to have that database.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where is that incorporated in the report? Can you help me with that. It's paragraph 3.0, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me check, Your Honour. It may be -- yes, I mean, the report does make reference to the database --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That particular page or part seems to be missing from the report, unless -- oh, unless -- no, I think what it does is identify the database as consisting of a number of sources. Is that correct? Do you have a copy of your report available, Mr. Riedlmayer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The database was submitted both in CD form and hard copy and it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let me take this just stage by stage, please. Do you have your report available?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it's at the end here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you go to what's called appendix 3, but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, in the index at the beginning, the table of contents, section 3 is entitled "Use of Database."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And then when you go to section 3 you get what's called appendix 3, "Allegations of Destruction" --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- is that different?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is different. That is A3. This is 3.0, which is on page 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Page 10, sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So thus the database becomes part of your report; is that the position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is part of the report, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, when you reflect in any -- in relation to any property, the information given to you by an informant or, as you've described it, local resident, who was it that obtained that information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were standing at the mosque site, taking pictures, and he stepped forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, but who obtained the information? Was it -- you've given us two names today working on this report, yourself and Mr. Herscher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The two of us would be there and one of us would note down the information and the particulars of the person who had given it to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And did you always work together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We always did, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And did you rely, for the source of these statements that you referred to, on anyone else other than you two gathering these statements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. We collected no second-hand reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ivetic, this is clearly entirely different from either As Seen, As Told or Under Orders, with this exception that the parts of Mr. Abrahams, the parts of Mr. Abrahams material that we did admit was very similar in nature to what's being described here by Mr. Riedlmayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, what I would indicate is, if you look at the investigation the corroborating report - and here it's media accounts - is from other parties who are not persons with whom Mr. Riedlmayer had contact. For instance, there is an Abdullah Mulaku, who is cited --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just give me a second until I get back to this page. Which --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The part I'm talking about now is at K0209393, is the number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just hold on a second until I get it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's under the media accounts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We are, as a Trial Chamber, very conscious of the difficulties associated with relying at all on media accounts, but it's interesting that, in his evidence so far, Mr. Riedlmayer said that they never used media as an exclusive source for determining anything in this; they used media principally as indicators of dates and then worked around other material.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I agree. I agree. I would also point out that, whereas this particular one for Vucitrn, which is why I paused before objecting, does list the informant name and was someone whom Mr. Riedlmayer spoke with, there are others where there is no informant listed or the information was obtained from other sources. So that's something that we might be a little bit more able to see if we go through more of the evidence and see what else he has to offer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think we're going to have to build up an attitude to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you're going to have to take specific objections if you feel there is a solid basis for them. But I've got two comments to make. One is the one to repeat what has already been said about putting materials, such as media reports, in the context that Mr. Riedlmayer puts it; and secondly, that no objection was taken under Rule 94 to the relevance of any of the material in this report when objections were taken generally to expert reports, so I wasn't anticipating this particular objection arising. However, we will repel the objection to this particular piece of material, but let's see if there are more fundamental points to be taken later which we can then consider. It's now time for our first break, Mr. Riedlmayer. The usher will show you where to wait. If you could leave the courtroom just now, and then we'll see you again in about 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, while we're waiting for the witness to come in, can I explain a little to answer part of your question, I think, about the exhibit. Exhibit 177 -- 1789 has his written report, plus it has photographs and the pages from the database that pertain to these individual mosques that we're talking about now. So there's some duplication that this exhibit, that we were looking at the break, 1788, are pages from the database concerning the mosque in Vucitrn. But those pages -- that page range, K0209391 to 9393, is contained among those items that are included in Exhibit P1789. That's my understanding in the Milosevic trial, the entire database was submitted. And I think what happened was we went through and copied those pages that pertained to these particular mosques, and then they were given ERNs. The database itself was not given a complete set of ERN numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But what is your proposal about its status for this trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm at the Court's discretion, because I understand the Court's ruling in other cases might be consistent with us only presenting the evidence about these mosques. I would have an argument to make that the evidence regarding the other sites of cultural destruction are relevant for other purposes, to show that there was a widespread and systematic pattern of behaviour here; that the damage that was done in these cases is not random or accidental, in light of the number and nature of the damages done in other cases; to show the fairness and objectivity of this expert in terms of the report, because it shows the damages they investigated regarding Serb and -- Serb Orthodox and Catholic sites --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll come back to that, Mr. Hannis. But can I take it that these individual pages that do have numbers on the 65 ter intimation, and which are part of what you've compiled as P1789, relate to the named locations in subparagraph (d) of 77.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: They do. But there are a few additional items contained under 1789 that refer to, I think, the extract that has examples of damage to Serb and Catholic structures as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Let's continue with the evidence meanwhile.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.
